_note: How the shop behaves in the simulator (sim/). Every rate here is an assumption chosen to sit near what the generated five-year history shows (about 0.4 contacts per order, 5% returns, 1% complaints); change a number and re-run. The business itself is described by this file, data/staff.json, data/costs.json, data/prospects.json and the world in data/world/<size>/. To describe a different business, give the simulator another set of these files (--data <folder>).

basket_top_up._note: Assumption (sim/top-up.mjs): a standard-delivery basket at or above near_share of the free-delivery threshold gets one more item to reach it with chance rate. Surveys (UPS/comScore Pulse of the Online Shopper, 2012-2015, from memory, not checked) put shoppers who say they have ever done this at about half; 0.3 per near basket is a judgement below that. Set rate to 0 to turn it off.

contacts._why_social: Share of contacts that arrive as social messages or public mentions instead of the channel drawn first. Assumption: UK small online shops report most help by email and chat, with social a minority (roughly 5 to 10%); the split between private messages and public tags is ours. Staff treat them like chats and check the social inboxes about hourly (pickup_minutes).
contacts._why_rates: Retuned 22 Nov 2026 so an untouched business gets about 0.2 contacts per order over time (published e-commerce figures run 0.19 to 0.46 tickets per order by category, https://www.eesel.ai/blog/ecommerce-support-contact-rate ; where-is-my-order about 4% of orders, https://www.retailbrew.com/stories/why-wismo-matters-and-how-dr-squatch-improved-theirs). Per-order totals: where is my order about 4%, damaged 1.5%, missing 0.5%, fault 1%, return question 4%, change order 2%, product and pre-sale questions 6%; late parcels and complaints on top. The daily rates are those totals spread over the days each kind of contact can happen. Assumptions apart from the two cited figures.
contacts._why_pickup: Minutes before a free person picks up a new message, by channel: chat and calls are watched, the mailbox is checked every hour or so. Assumption.

reviews._why_rate: Retuned 22 Nov 2026 to the generated history: about 8% of orders get a review in a week (28 reviews from 333 orders in the last four weeks of the standard world), counting the extra reviews after bad experiences. Assumption tied to our own history.

customer_model._note: Used only by the rich customer model (live sandboxes; --rich-customers in pnpm sim). Repeat buying follows the BG/NBD idea: each customer has their own buying rate (gamma across people) and, after each purchase, a chance of dropping out for good (beta across people). New customers arrive to replace natural dropouts, more with more marketing and a better reputation. Hidden traits and a manner for messages are drawn once per customer from the population seed and never shown through the engine's tools. Every number here is an assumption unless a source is given.
customer_model._source: Fader, Hardie and Lee (2005), Counting your customers the easy way: an alternative to the Pareto/NBD model. https://www.brucehardie.com/papers/bgnbd_2004-04-20.pdf . The shapes below are ours, not fitted.
customer_model._why_kinds: heterogeneity is the gamma shape of buying rates within a kind (low = a few people buy most); dropout_a and dropout_b give the beta spread of the chance of stopping for good after a purchase (mean a / (a + b): gift 12%, regular 4%, business 1.5%). Assumptions.
customer_model._why_acquisition: New customers arrive at the rate that replaces natural dropouts at the start, times the marketing push and reputation, raised to this power. Assumption.
customer_model._why_traits: Spread (log-normal sd) of each customer's price sensitivity, patience and tendency to leave around 1; share who complain in public after a bad experience. Hidden from tools, as CEO-Bench hides willingness to pay (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.18543). Assumptions.
customer_model._why_manner: Share of customers who describe things vaguely, who leave out their order number, and their tone. Simulated users that are all cooperative make tools look better than they are (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.11245v1; tau-trait https://arxiv.org/html/2510.04491v3). Assumptions.
